scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Dance of the Hornbill and the Warrior
This is Ngajat. 16th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Ngajat · Malaysia · 16th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated from Iban ancestors observing the common hill myna and the great argus, leading to the creation of 'Bungai Ajat' and 'Bunga Ajat' movements.
It is believed to be associated with the Iban ethnic group since the 16th century.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Ngajat is performed for Gawai harvest festivals, to welcome guests, and historically to celebrate the return of warriors.
It serves as a manifestation of masculinity, strength, and community identity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by graceful, bird-like movements.
Male dancers perform with shields and swords, often swinging their bodies.
Female dancers use the Pua Kumbu fabric as a central display.
Watch for Bungai Ajat, Ngajat Lesong.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers stand in a circle or move in a procession.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical ensemble includes large and medium gongs (tawak and bebendai), drums (ketebung/dumba), a set of small gongs (engkromong), and the belikan string instrument.
Listen for the tawak, bebendai, ketebung, dumba.

The music is driven by the interplay of large and medium gongs (tawak and bebendai) providing a deep, resonant foundation, punctuated by the rhythmic beat of drums (ketebung/dumba) and the melodic, high-pitched ringing of the engkromong small gongs.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Male dancers wear 'gagung' (thick vests of animal skin) and feathered headdresses.
Female dancers wear 'ngepan' headdresses, chest hooks, and bracelets.
Performances often take place on the 'tanju' (outer platform) of a longhouse or on a stage.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dion Das Louis, an eight-year-old dancer from Sarawak who won two gold medals at the 2024 World Performing Arts Championships.

Variants include Ngajat Serakup (standardized stage version), Ngajat Bebunoh (warrior/hunting replication), Ngajat Lesong (strength display), Ngajat Induk (female-led ritual), and Ngajat Ngalu Temuai (welcome dance).
The dance is a traditional Iban practice, with modern stage versions like Ngajat Serakup developed by the Dayak Dance and Cultural Association.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Certain rituals, such as those involving the Pua Kumbu and the welcoming of warriors, are deeply tied to ancestral offerings and spiritual protection; outsiders should observe with respect and avoid interrupting ritual processes.
